problem: Section 1 places the four layers below read() as system-call interface, I/O subsystem, device driver and interrupt handler, with the user process above them. The Q1 answer instead counts 'user-space I/O' as one of the four and says the interrupt handler 'sits with the driver', so the quiz contradicts the text the student just read. A student would not know whether the interrupt handler is a layer or not.
fix: Answer: the four software layers between the user process and the hardware are the system-call interface, the device-independent I/O subsystem, the device drivers and the interrupt handlers; hardware (controller plus device) is below these. The user-space library such as stdio is part of the user process, above the layers.

problem: 'Nonblocking keeps the CPU busy' is too broad. A nonblocking call by itself does not burn CPU; cost appears when the process polls in a loop. As written, students may think nonblocking I/O always wastes CPU.
fix: 'Nonblocking returns at once, so a process that polls in a loop keeps the CPU busy; used without polling, it lets the program do other work.'

problem: The formula T = h × T_cache + (1 − h) × T_device assumes a cache miss costs only the device access time. On a real miss the cache is also probed first, so the miss term is (T_cache + T_device). The chapter never states this assumption, and the worked examples then look like exact truth.
fix: Keep the formula but add one sentence: 'This assumes the miss costs only the device access; if the cache probe is also paid on a miss, the miss term becomes (1 − h) × (T_cache + T_device).'
